title: Introduction
text: Binary search is one of the most fundamental algorithms in programming.
It is a searching algorithm used to find a particular value in a sorted collection, such as an array.
Instead of checking every element one at a time, it repeatedly examines the middle element and uses that comparison to decide which half of the collection could contain the target.
This allows binary search to find values much more efficiently than a linear search if the required conditions are met.

title: How it works
text: Instead of iterating through every element one by one, binary search exploits an attribute called monotonicity.
It begins by looking at the middle element of the sorted array. If the middle element is the target, the search is complete.
If the target is greater than the middle element, the algorithm continues searching only the right half because every value on the left is guaranteed to be too small.
If the target is smaller, it searches only the left half following the same principle. The process repeats until the target is found or no elements remain.
Because half of the remaining elements are removed after every comparison, binary search takes logarithmic time, written as O(log n).
For example, in an array of size 1'000'000'000, binary search checks at most about 30 elements, which is significantly fewer than 1'000'000'000.

title: When to use it
text: Binary search can only be used when the data is ordered in a way that lets us eliminate half of the search space after each comparison.
The most common example is a sorted array of numbers, where smaller values appear before larger values.
The collection should also allow direct access to its middle elements.
Binary search is useful when searching through a large, already sorted collection.
It cannot be applied directly to an unsorted array. The data must be sorted first.
